AI spend is nowhere close to hitting any walls. Obviously this data is weighted toward engineering-centric companies, with the top 1% spending $7,500/mo and top 10% spending $660/mo per employee on AI. But the general trend of continued exponential growth is occurring throughout all firm types. 

And what the top 10% is doing today may easily be what the top 50% is doing in 3 years from now, at least in terms of token volume if not in dollars. This is why there’s still so much opportunity right now in the diffusion of AI in the enterprise.

Especially as token costs come down, we will throw larger portions of work at agents. They’ll be scanning all our code for security issues, testing all of our software, writing coding for much larger projects, processing nearly all data, and much more. So this trend has no end in sight.

Pretty good way to think about the value of AI agents and where the opportunity lies. You have a technology that will tirelessly do all the things that you could never fully do before. Not because you didn’t want to or it wasn’t valuable, but because it was just not even remotely practical.

The upside with AI is to think about everything you can now throw intelligence at that won’t give up and what would the returns be. 

You just couldn’t possibly find every security vulnerability in your codebase, because you couldn’t simulate every risk vector. You couldn’t read every contract or document to process the data and capture it to query later. You couldn’t comb through your customer base and look for every relevant data point for doing upsells. And so on. 

This is a pretty clear way to think about how to deploy AI to get real gains, but also where the startup opportunities are as well. Go after the markets where more compute on a problem will qualitatively change what customers can now do in that domain.

1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation.

First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice.  I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world.  Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people.  I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of.  But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes.  A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice.  At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power.

This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully.  We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors.  California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that).  More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers.  Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up.  This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights!

Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws).  Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers).  By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring.

BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”.  The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure.  I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity.  This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either.

The argument that “AI structurally centralizes power” because it’s currently compute hungry ignores 125 years of super exponential growth in compute price-performance. 

Improvement in algorithms and continued hardware efficiency gains     means there is no reason to assume AGI-level capabilities will always require a data center to run.

Scaling laws are not laws of physics. They’re simply empirical relationships observed for particular architectures, objectives, datasets etc. Change any one of those factors and you get a different scaling curve. 

If the brain is any guide, true AGI will likely be very efficient. In fact, current scaling laws might a bug and not a feature. It shows how inefficiency of the ML algorithms we discovered so far.

tweets.text: The conflation of “regulation” and “regulatory capture” in AI discourse has always been frustrating to me. It is hard to have a reasonable conversation about public policy when half of the commentariat conflates all AI-specific public policy ideas with “regulatory capture.”

AI policy debate on this site really does feel stuck in an endlessly repeating first principles debate about “whether” we should “regulate AI.” The conversation here has not meaningfully evolved since the battle lines hardened with SB 1047 (or maybe the Biden EO).

But meanwhile the world has moved on. Laws have passed, EOs signed, and both are now in their implementation stages rather than the planning. People are figuring out how it’s all going to work, bit by bit, imperfectly, and with deep ambiguity at every corner. Nonetheless, a legal regime of AI governance is gradually emerging from both the state and federal level. It can’t not emerge; the risks are too real, it’s too obvious to too many of the adults who remain in the room.

It’s still very nascent, yet it is clearly happening, and it is clearly not being shaped very much by discourse on this website. Twitter is said to be “the global town square,” the place to be for relevance. Not so for AI policy. 

There used to be niche policy nerd communities here who would talk among themselves, and while that does exist in AI policy, the real conversations in this community occur off the feed. 

I don’t like this state of affairs. I wish it weren’t so. It’d be better if there was a robustly informed public debate on these issues. And to be clear, you can still keep track; there are public events, podcasts, papers, Substacks, etc. Most of the interesting ideas are out there being discussed and debated, just mostly in niche forums. 

But right now, here in the “global town square,” the impression one gets about what is going on in AI policy is about as good of the impression of the world you’d have gotten from reading Slate in 2017, or the New York Times opinion page in the summer of 2020 (and indeed, as Joe has observed, the woke mafia has returned; same tactics, different people and issues. These are probably related phenomena). 

For young writers and policy entrepreneurs, this website is still probably important to get your name out there, at least for now. And it’s still important, for policy purposes, to track sentiment around particular models, companies, people etc. on the timeline. There is still some signal to be extracted, though you may be able to automate much of that extraction now. This, of course, ends with AIs mining for signal from other AIs, which, if we’re being honest, is probably already a huge part of what this site has become.

introducing /vision. it's a very simple skill to help you write down an explicit VISION.md file for your project

but what's VISION.md? as we let agents do more and more work for us, we have to remove ourselves as a bottleneck, and evolve the way we influence their work

we began by carefully reviewing and controlling the code written by agents, but soon there's just too much to read

we then shifted to discussing detailed plans with the agents, as most of the time if the plan is right, the agents can get it implemented

what i've been experiencing for the past couple of months is telling me that eventually we won't even be able to review all the plans

imagine your project is getting 1000 feature requests from customers each day, which ones do you implement vs reject? who has the time review 1000 plans a day to make those judgment calls?

our influence has to go one level up - we need to define the vision. a vision is not about what the project currently is, but about where do we want it to go. when a new idea comes up, the vision statement is what decides whether the idea fits with the project or not

this /vision skill itself is very simple, but i think it's an important philosophy we need to adopt because that's the next layer of abstraction many of us have to go into, in order to continue to scale

the skill currently looks at what's already been done in the project to build context, and would then propose 8-12 hypothetical borderline feature ideas, to really challenge your thinking on where you'd like the project to go and force clarity. then it'll take all that into account and write down the VISION.md file

you can then use the file to triage feature ideas, detect implementation drift during code review, or help make ambiguous product decisions that pop up from time to time

check it out https://t.co/pZBFxHgJ5a and you can see an example of VISION.md defined in the firstmate project https://t.co/8j4chaR1Bs 

still quite early and can be improved a lot, but since it's getting attention i thought i should make a proper introduction. let me know what you think or if you have any questions!
